correctness.rationale: For small r, the length measure of metric balls gives P(D<=r)=2r/L+O(r^2), recovering L. Four simple endpoint/other-arm routes bound the diameter by (b+c)/2, attained by midpoints on those two arms, hence a=L-2d*. Set epsilon=d*-r. On b,c arms, variables p=x+y-(b+c)/2 and q=x-y-(b-c)/2 satisfy |p|<epsilon, |q|<a+epsilon plus domain |p+q|<b, |p-q|<c, with Jacobian 1/2. For epsilon<=(b-a)/2 the rectangle is uncut and both orders have tail measure 4epsilon(a+epsilon). At the first onset h=(b-a)/2 the same-long-arm and short-long-arm contributions enter with positive linear 2(a+c)delta (doubled when b=c); old b,c corner-clipping affects only O(delta^2), making the threshold sharp. For a=b<c the distinct-arm and same-arm leading slope is 2c+6a, and for a=b=c it is 12a, both >4a. Thus the slope classifies ties and the first exact-law breakpoint identifies b otherwise, completing inversion for all real triples. Inspected rational polygon-clipping verifier checks finite parameter cases, but proof is analytic.

value.rationale: A global inverse theorem is mathematically meaningful because distance histograms fail injectivity on arbitrary metric-measure spaces. This exact three-arm classification and constructive inversion, including collisions of arm lengths, is a distinct natural finite-dimensional identifiability result; no downstream theorem is needed to justify the classification.

limitations: Exactly three strictly positive arms and normalized arclength; no stability claim for finitely sampled histograms.
Cannot extend from local injectivity to global uniqueness without the explicit breakpoint proof.
